title: Ernest Milton's band and the Depression, 1933-37
summary: He joined Milton about 1933-34 for three or four years; pay collapsed and he quit.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Yeah, they were all over the country. Yeah. I remember. And your last band, was that with Milton again that you were working with? You mentioned Buddy Petit playing second. Is that after De Pass?
Yeah, it was after De Pass. Yeah, yeah. When Buddy was there with Milton, I wasn't playing with Milton.
No, I wasn't playing with him. I got with him after that. I think I got with Ernest Milton on about 34. 33 or 34. Yeah, I was playing with Milton.
Yeah, Buddy Petit was dead then.

Yeah. Yeah. About 33 or 34, I started playing with Milton. We played together about three or four years. Oh. And that's, that run out. Music was absolutely nothing. You got around, when you getting down playing music, you got a man to change a dollar and play, and you know that was tough. Yeah. I remember once, I got a little job there for this lottery man there on Hawks, that jury man on Stephen All Street. He had a little dance at a, you know, had a band that come play there for his lottery. I think I charged him a dollar. He said, Sam, for Joe Nickles and Mealy Bone and them Nick, they take me down for six bits. I said, I said, it's time to quit now. Yeah. Yeah. Well, I went that, he was that. Watch told me, he said, well, you men, you got a dollar man, you got five, now I can take six bits. He started going to play every six bits. I said, Mr. Hart, please tell him he could have it. Thing was rough. Yeah, that's right. That's the thing that's really rough. So I went to waiting for a contract that he used to make a couple of days a week. I stayed with him until I got this job by Black Wyatt, Douglas. I put my horn up, not put it up, I'll give it to my nephew.
